children: Across India’s business families, the next generation faces a defining test: turning inherited scale into new engines of growth, with a founder’s ambition and the discipline to make capital count

Every generation of Indian business inheritors faces the same question dressed in the clothes of its era. In the ‘licence raj’ years, it was whether the sons of industrialists could navigate a state-controlled economy. In the liberalisation decade, it was whether they could compete against multinationals rushing in. Today, the question is sharper and more fundamental than either of those.
Can the heirs become founders again?

This is what the current transitions at Ambani, Birla and Jindal are actually testing, even if the business press has framed it in gentler ways. Beyond these western conglomerates, the question travels through financial services in Delhi, beverages in Gurugram, automotive manufacturing in Chennai and batteries in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.

Truly great business dynasties are those that preserve wealth but also repeatedly create new engines of growth across generations. Dhirubhai Ambani founded one empire. Mukesh Ambani, inheriting petrochemicals and a fraternal feud, arguably built a second through Jio, using the cash flows of a commodity business to disrupt an entire industry. Can Akash, Isha and Anant build a third?

Together they constitute a disproportionate share of India’s industrial identity. Together they are in transition simultaneously. What that transition produces will shape Indian capitalism for the next quarter century.
Ambani: The Architecture of a Third Empire

Mukesh Ambani’s handling of succession is, by any measure, among the most structurally deliberate in Indian corporate history. The template is clean: assign business verticals to the next generation, retain the commodities engine as a funding mechanism and maintain the patriarch’s active guidance.

Akash Ambani leads technology businesses, Isha leads consumer businesses and Anant leads energy businesses. Each has been given a genuine business with a real P&L, real competition and scrutiny from public markets watching every quarterly result. Boards and professional managers remain part of that accountability.

The scale is extraordinary. Reliance Retail recorded gross revenue of Rs 3,70,026 crore in FY26. By June 2026, its registered customer base exceeded 396 million. Jio has crossed 500 million subscribers. But numbers are the easy part of the story. The harder question is what the numbers are obscuring.

Reliance Retail’s EBITDA margin slipped from 8.7 per cent to 7.9 per cent year on year in Q1 FY27, with management attributing the compression to digital commerce investment. Isha Ambani is not presiding over a smooth growth arc. She is fighting Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart in a sector where growth comes with demanding economics. The consumer transition is real, the competition is real, and the outcome is genuinely uncertain.

Anant’s new energy mandate is the most grandiose in its articulation and the longest in its horizon. Reliance says the business has entered accelerated commissioning and early revenues. The question now is whether the manufacturing ecosystem at Jamnagar can translate enormous investment into competitive products and durable returns. Announced capacity and commercial achievement are different milestones.

The Ambani succession is structurally well planned. The heirs’ initiative is impressive. Each has been handed a founding problem inside an inherited structure. Akash must grow Jio from a telecom platform into the consumer operating system of a billion people. Isha must build a physical-digital retail ecosystem that can serve consumers from Mumbai apartments to smaller-town kirana stores. Anant can fuel India for the new world.
These are founding challenges. Will the inheritance accelerate or inhibit the founding instinct?
Birla: Founding at the Edges

Kumar Mangalam Birla is preparing his children through board immersion before full command, the path he himself walked when he inherited a $2 billion empire at age 28. Aryaman and Ananya were inducted onto the boards of Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail in 2023 and Hindalco in 2024.

The founding moves at the edges of the empire are more instructive than the board appointments. Birla Opus, launched in 2024 with Rs 10,000 crore in committed capital, is a greenfield consumer brand creation inside an industrial conglomerate. Grasim now places it third in India’s organised decorative paints industry, reporting revenue of Rs 1,661 crore in Q1 FY27. The group has accepted significant financial pain for consumer positioning. Whether that pain becomes a war chest or a millstone depends on execution discipline. This remains a group investment, not an achievement attributable to the heirs alone.

The RCB acquisition tells a different story about the next generation specifically. A consortium led by Aditya Birla Group agreed to acquire Royal Challengers Bengaluru for $1.78 billion, naming Aryaman Vikram Birla chairman. Aryaman, a former first-class cricketer, brings genuine domain knowledge. The stated ambition of building RCB into a global sports institution is the right level of aspiration for a $1.78 billion investment. The risk is that franchise valuations at this level leave almost no margin for sentiment to outrun business reality. The team must win and a chairman must show what institution building looks like beyond brand association.

Ananya Birla is among the most independently credible figures in the cohort. She founded Svatantra Microfin at seventeen. Her entrepreneurial identity preceded her formal entry into the group’s structures. That independence is an important signal in the Birla succession. It demonstrates the instinct to create a business, even as the advantages accompanying the family name remain considerable.
Jindal: The Discipline of the Focused Founder

Parth Jindal has articulated the founding logic most explicitly and executed it most methodically, which makes the JSW story both the cleanest case study and the most useful test of whether the logic holds under scrutiny. That said, vanity and scale are cousins.

Parth’s diagnosis was structural. JSW, for all its industrial scale, needed stronger recognition at the consumer level. Steel was a commodity. To become a consumer choice, JSW needed to become a consumer brand first. That required a different kind of capital and it was all about brand investment.

JSW Sports was the calculated response. Through interests in Delhi Capitals, Bengaluru FC and Haryana Steelers, the group connected its name with audiences beyond its industrial customers. The rub-off effect on JSW Paints and JSW Cement as B2C brands was deliberate. Sports as brand infrastructure. It is the most creative strategic logic in the cohort.

The paints transaction then took the pivot to scale. In June 2025, JSW Paints agreed to acquire AkzoNobel’s 74.76 per cent stake in its Indian subsidiary for up to Rs 8,986 crore, gaining access to Dulux. JSW Cement went public in August 2025. JSW One Platforms extends the group’s reach into business-to-business commerce.

The logic chain of steel slag as cement input, distribution as a platform for adjacent products, sports as brand capital, brand capital as consumer preference is genuinely fitting. The risk, which the elegance of the theory slightly obscures, is that Dulux is an acquired brand equity, not a created one. Acquiring brand equity is not the same as building it. The task is to justify the purchase price while strengthening consumer preference.
Beyond The Western Conglomerates

In Gurugram, Varun Jaipuria, executive vice-chairman of Varun Beverages, brings an operating mandate to the succession story. The company credits him with acquisitions and the integration of acquired territories. The inherited advantage is the PepsiCo bottling platform. The founding challenge is to reproduce its operating strengths across new markets without assuming that distribution, consumer demand and returns travel automatically together.

Delhi’s Jai Bajaj represents an earlier stage. His mandate at Bajaj Capital is to turn a longstanding financial advisory business into a technology-, data- and AI-enabled financial-planning institution. The inherited asset is client trust. The opportunity is to make advice more accessible and personalised. The outcome remains to be established; a new mandate is the beginning of the story, not evidence of its success.

In Chennai, Sudarshan Venu, chairman and managing director of TVS Motor, is building on a manufacturing institution while pursuing electric mobility and a global premium motorcycle business through Norton. The company credits him with international expansion. Norton makes the founding question tangible: can an acquired British marque become a competitive global business? Heritage attracts attention. Products, distribution and returns must sustain it.

At Amara Raja, executive director Vikramadithya Gourineni’s new energy responsibilities confront a different transition. A family business built around lead-acid batteries must establish capabilities in lithium-ion cells and energy storage. Its planned 16 GWh gigafactory in Telangana signals the scale of that commitment. The inherited customer relationships help, but a different chemistry demands new technology, manufacturing competence and cost competitiveness. Here, renewal requires building beyond the technology that created the legacy.

Kolkata offers another variation. Shashwat Goenka, vice-chairman of RP-Sanjiv Goenka Group, has helped develop its consumer businesses, including Too Yumm. His challenge is to build brands that earn repeat purchases and profits, rather than merely broaden the list of sectors in which the family operates.
The Alternative Model: What Tata Teaches
The most instructive counterpoint to the family succession model is not a failed business. It is the most respected conglomerate in India.

The Tata model is a dual architecture with the Trusts providing values, governance and long-term orientation while professional management leads commercial strategy. Codified governance performs the role of a living patriarch. The result is an organisation that retains patient capital and institutional credibility while accessing professional talent and operational discipline.

But there is a difference between a model and a guarantee. The Trust architecture separates philanthropic ownership from commercial operation. Founders pass specific mandates. Trustees pass principles. The gap between the two is where value can be destroyed if accountability is unclear.

The pressure at Bombay House makes that gap visible. In April, The Times of India reported internal estimates of up to Rs 29,000 crore in FY26 losses across newer ventures, against an earlier projection of Rs 5,700 crore. These were reported estimates, not a disclosed combined audited result.

N. Chandrasekaran’s third-term decision was deferred in February. He subsequently announced that he would not seek reappointment when his term ends in February 2027. Noel Tata’s more assertive oversight shows that patient capital is not infinitely patient. Professional management needs a long runway, but also clear milestones and scrutiny.

Noel’s son Neville was appointed a trustee of the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust in November 2025. Family participation is visible within the governance structure, although trusteeship is not personal ownership of the charitable assets.

Can heirs combine the founding instinct that family ownership enables with the institutional discipline that the Tata model has demonstrated? One without the other produces either inspired incompetence or competent stagnation.
The Real Test of Capital Allocation

Strip away the PR agency-pitched succession narratives, the Ivy League degrees, the cosmopolitan attitude, the global circuit citizenship, the IPL franchises, the Forbes citations and the AGM announcements.
Look at capital allocation.

The founding question is ultimately a question about where they choose to put money. Preservers allocate to the core and defend margins, protect market share, maintain the machine. Founders allocate to the new, accepting that new engines of growth require long-duration, loss-tolerating investment that markets penalise in the short term.
Mukesh Ambani built Jio. Kumar Mangalam Birla committed capital to build a consumer brand from scratch. Sajjan Jindal scaled up steel and established the operating mindset of his enterprises.
These are founding decisions, not management ones. The heirs inherited their consequences. What the next generation must now demonstrate is that they can make the next founding allocation.

Deployment courage is a test of nerves. What a founder does when the allocation was wrong is a test of character. What will they do when the bet disappoints, when the market turns, when the early numbers do not come?

Each must identify the next engine, commit capital to it before the outcome is clear and sustain the conviction when the early numbers disappoint. Equally, they must recognise when the evidence demands a change of course, however uncomfortable.
That is what founding looks like. The inheritance is the licence to attempt it.
Look for the achievement not in press releases, but in P&Ls.
Dr. Annurag Batra

BW Reporters Dr Annurag Batra is Chairman and Editor-in-Chief of BW Businessworld and Founder of the exchange4media Group. A first-generation entrepreneur and media leader, he is also an angel investor, author, television host and mentor to entrepreneurs and media professionals. He serves on several corporate and institutional boards and has a longstanding association with management education.

An alumnus of MDI Gurgaon, he has served on its Board of Governors and as President of the MDI Alumni Association. He is also a member of the International Academy of Television Arts & Sciences.
